prompt.brief: Design a secure wire-transfer API for domestic and international payments with beneficiary verification, sanctions/fraud controls, multi-step approval, settlement tracking, and immutable auditability.
successSignals: Define transfer intent/state machine, source/destination accounts, beneficiary, limits, fees/FX, compliance decisions, settlement, returns, and idempotency.
Keep ledger reservation and authorization correct while external bank rails remain asynchronous; reconcile unknown outcomes rather than retrying blindly.
Separate API orchestration from double-entry ledger, sanctions/fraud checks, bank adapters, approvals, notifications, and reconciliation.
Explain maker-checker controls, encryption, audit retention, provider failure, duplicate messages, privacy, observability, and pending status.

functional: Create and authorize domestic/international transfers, verify beneficiaries, screen sanctions/fraud, reserve funds, submit to rails, and track settlement.
Support approvals, fees/FX, cutoff windows, status webhooks, returns/recalls, reconciliation, statements, and compliance reporting.
Make retries idempotent, preserve a balanced ledger and audit trail, enforce role limits, and recover safely from rail timeouts or duplicates.
nonFunctional: Return an accepted/pending/failed result within two seconds while guaranteeing no duplicate debit or credit ledger effect.
Scale to 1M transfers per day across accounts and corridors without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 1M transfers/day, 100k webhook events/hour, and multi-currency corridors
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Secure wire-transfer API commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Secure wire-transfer API writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Secure wire-transfer API version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Secure wire-transfer API by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Secure wire-transfer API work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Secure wire-transfer API projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Secure wire-transfer API projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Secure wire-transfer API records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Secure wire-transfer API latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
